extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, researchers studying peer-review practices, and academic policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for assessing manuscripts and the peer-review/editing process, including reviewer competence, bias (identity/affiliation effects), methodological rigor, editorial procedures, and proposed remedies (blind review, paid review, alternative publication models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / real-world importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Results should be of significance to anyone in the real world; fascinating problems and satisfying solutions are insufficient if they lack broader significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors cannot create significance on their own; without significance, results (e.g., 'test number 6 of hypothesis X from laboratory Y') are unlikely to be long remembered even by field specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity (accuracy) of reviewing, not just reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the validity of reviewing (are assessments correct?) rather than solely on interreviewer reliability (agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement between reviewers does not guarantee correctness — reviewers may agree yet be wrong (Peters & Ceci demonstration). Emphasize validating reviewers' judgments against objective measures where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of reviewer bias from author identity and affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial evaluation must be unbiased by information about authors' identity, reputation, or institutional affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peters & Ceci demonstrated that knowledge of author identity/affiliation can shift recommendations; journals should consider procedures to mitigate such halo/status effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent application of acceptance criteria across author statuses (discriminability vs criterion shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should apply the same acceptance criteria regardless of author status; differences should reflect manuscript quality (discriminability) not shifting thresholds (criterion effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary notes reviewers may attend more to methodological defects for low-status authors (discriminability) rather than applying defects equally but rejecting low-status authors more often (criterion shift). Evaluate whether reviewers weight characteristics differently by author status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor: research design, methodology, and data analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should report a sound research design, appropriate methodology, and correct data analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characteristics were cited as prominent grounds for recommendation/rejection; poor methodology/analysis are primary justifications for rejecting resubmitted manuscripts in the P&C study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial processing fairness: distribution to reviewers and weighting of recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should distribute manuscripts fairly to reviewers and apply consistent, transparent weighting to reviewers' recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors do not distribute manuscripts randomly nor weight recommendations equally; editorial selection and follow-up actions can be a major source of bias independent of individual reviewer criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer competence and appropriateness (expertise match)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must be competent and appropriate matches to the manuscript's specialized research interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P&C's results may reflect editors' mistaken beliefs about reviewers' specialized interests; competence/appropriateness can be assessed via analysis of editorial records (e.g., whether reviewers recognized published articles in their areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical auditing of editorial steps and reviewer recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use editors' files and records to empirically establish whether editorial steps (distribution, follow-up) favor specific categories of authors and to identify determinants of editorial board composition and reviewer recruitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' records can enable rigorous assessments of selective practices; analyses should examine distribution patterns and follow-up behavior to detect systematic favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and potential corruption of blind reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind reviewing has virtues but also limits: editors often remain unblinded, and skilled authors can indirectly reveal identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blind review should be evaluated carefully — it may reduce some biases but be vulnerable to identity cues; also, authors must be offered the option and editors need to consider requiring it to protect less prestigious authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reviewer/author sex interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether evaluations differ as a function of reviewer sex and author sex, accounting for task and situational interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence suggests men and women may judge women differently depending on context; analyses should consider interaction effects rather than assume uniform behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate experimental controls and research design in studies of peer-review bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies examining reviewer bias must include proper control conditions (e.g., resubmission permutations controlling for original status), adequate sample sizes, and avoidance of confounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators recommend designs that vary original and resubmission prestige symmetrically, include unpublished manuscripts, and check equivalence of reviewer demographics and competence; without such controls results are difficult to interpret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of citation impact as a validation metric for editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation counts (e.g., SSCI) may serve as an external criterion to assess whether preferential acceptance of high-status authors is justified by subsequent impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perlman used citation rates to argue that papers from high-status institutions were cited more (suggesting editors' preferential treatment may be rational); use impact metrics carefully and consider pluralistic citation patterns vs in-group self-citation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review format innovations to improve reliability (simultaneous rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve interrater reliability by having reviewers rate sets of papers simultaneously to provide a comparative framework rather than reviewing papers periodically over long spans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneous consideration provides salient comparisons and previously improved reliability in at least one study (McReynolds 1971).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policies for solicited commentaries (archival validity and editing rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicited commentaries should meet archival validity checks; journals reserve the right to edit for relevance/style, delete redundant portions, and prioritize order based on receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BBS instructions: 'all original data will be inferred in order to ensure the archival validity ... BBS also reserves the right to edit commentaries for relevance and style ... portions redundant ... may have to be deleted ... priority ... assigned in terms of order of receipt.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation for reviewers to improve review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay reviewers adequately for their time to increase responsibility, thoroughness, and impartiality in reviewing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paid reviews could incentivize better scrutiny; funding might come from authors' institutions or grants, though this imposes costs on authors and raises policy questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative publication models (open/post-publication review and machine-readable preprints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore interactive, post-publication commentary, machine-readable preprints, and integrated review/dissemination systems as alternatives to conventional pre-publication refereeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porter sketches a system where papers are made available as 'new research', automated usage counts and commentaries inform quality, authors can update papers in response to comments, and secondary journals synthesize important/controversial work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent record-keeping and usage metrics for assessing performance and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain records on accesses, comments, and review history; use tallies and feedback to evaluate scientific performance and reviewer/editor effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porter suggests providing tallies of how many people accessed articles and what comments were made; these metrics can serve as alternative measures of scientific performance beyond publication venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical standards for research on peer review (use of deception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess ethical acceptability of deceptive research designs (e.g., resubmitting published papers under false by-lines) when studying peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators raised ethical objections to Peters & Ceci's ploy; researchers must weigh scientific value against ethical concerns and consider safeguards/approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author appeal and editorial reconsideration mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should provide mechanisms for authors to protest decisions and for editors to reevaluate papers when injustice is alleged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors sometimes reevaluate after authors complain; providing a structured appeal process can correct errors and acknowledge the fallibility of the system.
